We also identify key challenges in current research, propose potential directions for future investigation, and suggest practical guidelines for selecting appropriate evaluation methods. Our analysis may aid scientists and engineers in selecting suitable uncertainty assessment methods and may contribute to the development of more reliable and interpretable AI systems.

We investigate the von Neumann algebra generated by category functions within an arbitrary compact quantum group, demonstrating that this function always falls under a specific operator, the dimension function, within that algebra. Furthermore, if the category functions generate a maximal subalgebra (equal to the entire algebra), then the associated quantum group symmetry is inherently rational. Additionally, for a wide range of compact quantum group types (including those based on a parameter), we examine the algebraic properties, dimensional structure, and embedding relationships with other known quantum group algebras.

This research introduces a refined strategy iteration method by incorporating fuzzy cuts on its maximization operator to handle extensive Markov decision processes with uncertain transition probabilities. The refined strategy iteration enhances convergence speed and provides analytical insights into the impact of uncertainty on convergence. A related variant of this method is also explored for stochastic games with absolute probability bounds. The proposed methods were tested on several randomly generated Markov processes and games to verify their correctness.

Let Q be a weighted directed graph with n vertices and no repeated edges. The edge ideal of Q, denoted as I(Q), can be represented as a monomial ideal in the polynomial ring S = K[x_1, ..., x_n], where each edge (u,v) is associated with a variable x and w(e) denotes the weight of edge e. The primary objective of this study is to identify the polar graphs of Q under specific conditions when the mixed elementary symmetric function of roots of a given polynomial has maximal degree. These conditions lead to the determination that the edge ideal of the polar graph of Q has a unique factorization into n linear factors.

This paper addresses the input identification challenge for time-series computer simulations through the evaluation of multiple time-based simulators at various points along contours. A primary method for resolving the input identification issue involves the comparison of time-series, which can be quantified by their correlations. Our approach extends this concept by generalizing it to any number of time-series, applicable to computer simulations with varying parameter values. The computational efficiency can be significantly improved by focusing on the extremes of correlation values, which can be computed in linear time using an algorithm based on Hu and Mainwaring's work. A step-by-step procedure is proposed for resolving the identification issue and validated on three computer models.

This study investigates how regional data can enhance the training of deep learning models. Multiple studies have demonstrated that training on specific regions of data can lead to superior performance compared to using the full dataset. However, the method of using full batches for gradient calculation may prevent effective regional learning due to insufficient exploitation of correlations between neighboring samples. To address this limitation, the authors propose RQNet, an innovative technique that utilizes the Euclidean distance between neighboring samples to generate sample-specific gradient updates when processing regional queries. Experimental results on standard benchmarks show that RQNet significantly outperforms existing methods like data augmentation and small-batch training. Notably, even without hyperparameter tuning, the strength of regional queries on specific datasets can yield a substantial improvement of over 5%.

The characterization of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) can be facilitated by jets with a high-transverse momentum relative to the collision axis, particularly those including a solitary isolated photon, as they offer minimal alteration by the QGP transverse momentum, thus serving as reference points, with their partners providing insights into the QGP modifications. To this end, measurements of fragmentation, both with and without isolated photons, were conducted using jets with transverse momenta ranging from 60 to 120 GeV, paired with isolated photons with transverse momenta above 100 GeV, in 2016 collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon-pair of 5.02 TeV in lead-lead collisions at the LHC, and compared to the proton-proton baseline. Results indicate that for jets aligned with an isolated photon, energy-loss is observed to be independent of $p_{T,~\rm jet}^{\rm pp}$, and less than for jets without isolated photons, at both  $p_{T,~\rm jet}^{\rm pp} =$ 60 and 120 GeV, suggesting energy loss of approximately 15% and 25% respectively. This study provides the most precise comparison to date of $e^{\gamma}$- and hadronic-jet-based fragmentation function suppressions.

Recent research involving hypergeometric series with parameters and multiple zeta values has been the focus of multiple papers, including those with Ap\'{e}ry-type properties. Building upon previous findings, this paper reveals new series representations featuring these properties. The authors derive novel identities related to hypergeometric series and determine corresponding mZV-expression, subsequently obtaining Ap\'{e}ry-type series as a result. A distinct advantage of the authors' approach相比 to that of Ruan is that it does not rely on mZV-expression with alternating signs. These new series representations are then applied to resolve long-standing conjectures put forth by Bradie, Crandall, and others.

A brown dwarf, detected in the field of 3CR J1534+13, was noted for its peculiar 2.2 micrometer variability and highly variable, polarized emission at 8 micrometer. Initially, this brown dwarf was thought to have a hot spot on its surface, causing the observed 2.2 micrometer variability through rotating emission through a surrounding disk, which also explained the polarized 8 micrometer reading. However, recent observations in the optical and near-infrared range have uncovered significant color variations, contradicting such a model and necessitating an alternative explanation. Further research, such as the multi-epoch photometry and spectroscopy, will be required to develop a comprehensive model of this object's observed emissions.

Produced in high energy particle collisions is a hot and dense state of matter called a "fireball." As this system expands and cools, various types of subatomic particles are created, including light and intermediate-mass hadrons and heavier resonances, providing insight into the complex forces at work within this environment. We present findings from the first rapid collisions of gold nuclei at an energy of 5.44 TeV per nucleon pair, conducted by the CERN STAR experiment.

We have developed a novel approach to interpolate, extrapolate, and extend parton distribution functions within a specific DGLAP evolution framework. Our method can also incorporate a Doplicher-Bradley type of n-parton function when available. A significant advantage of this framework is its ability to smoothly connect parts on different sides of the Bjorken-x=1 boundary without abrupt changes. Furthermore, this approach allows us to extend the functions into unexplored regions of x and x^2 by assuming their behavior is similar to that observed in neighboring measured areas. We applied this approach to extend CTEQ6 parton distribution functions beyond the domains covered by experimental data and our results are presented here.

Creating structures on the Moon and Mars using in-situ resources is a top priority for establishing a sustained presence in an extraterrestrial environment. Regolith, an extraterrestrial soil resource abundant on celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars, has great potential for use in 3D printing and other construction methods that rely on heat. Regolith binders that have undergone thermal processing show significantly improved mechanical attributes compared to their heatless counterparts. However, there have been no studies that analyze the effect of thermal processing heat on binders' properties. This study examined the impact of different sintering heat levels (300, 500, 700, 900, 1100, 1300, 1500, 1700, 1900, and 2100 degrees Celsius) on the binder binding capability. The findings revealed that the optimal sintering heat for both types of regolith was 500 degrees Celsius. At this heat level, the mechanical attributes of the binders reached their peak values and then began to decline as the heat increased. Furthermore, the mechanical attributes of Martian regolith binder were found to be superior to those of lunar regolith binder across the full heat spectrum. Analysis under an electron microscope and using XRD showed that the heat's influence led to the formation of specific mineral and amorphous substances that improved binder performance.

The impact of shear on the Rayleigh-Plateau instability in a hanging liquid film was investigated through both theoretical and experimental approaches. A linear stability analysis was employed, incorporating two types of shear: average film shear and boundary shear due to a moving substrate. The findings revealed that shear has a stabilizing effect, with films experiencing average shear being the most stable. In contrast, sheared layers can undergo the dripping phase transition at a slower decay rate, leading to an effective increase in the critical aspect ratio. Experiments conducted, simulating a range of shear conditions, were in agreement with theoretical models. Furthermore, a comparison with previous experimental and numerical results was discussed.

We have developed an effective method to derive star formation rates from the photometric modeling of the spectral energy distributions of the nearby star-forming galaxy Cederberg. Using the H$\beta$/Brackett$\gamma$ ratio, we determined the star formation rate and verified its accuracy through an independent analysis using the UV continuum, which yielded consistent results. This dual approach enabled us to assess the reliability of H$\beta$ derived from the Brackett$\gamma$ line, which is often affected by dust and other factors. The B$\gamma$ ratio has the advantage of minimizing uncertainties from intrinsic extinction, but may be more susceptible to line broadening or external contamination. Despite these potential issues, our analysis of other emission lines in Cederberg showed that the H$\beta$ rate derived from B$\gamma$ is a reliable indicator of star formation rates. This suggests that the B$\gamma$ ratio could be a valuable tool for measuring the star formation rates of distant galaxies, where H$\beta$ may be difficult to observe.

This paper explores the conformal field theory tied to $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ and its associated affine algebra at a fixed level $k$. It delves into the COV symmetry, a Y-bilinear quantum group associated with the affine algebra, that acts on its level-$k$ representations. A primary achievement lies in defining this action within the vertex operator algebra framework, allowing for explicit generation via conformal field theory methods. Furthermore, the study identifies the universal property underlying this action, enabling the construction of a homomorphism from the quantum group to the endomorphisms of the vacuum representation, an affiliation not found in existing literature.

The diffusion process is widely applied in various fields, including data analysis, signaling, and finance. Based on Brownian motion's statistical properties, it is typically analyzed using its ordinary differential equations. This paper presents an alternative method for solving the non-linear diffusion equation utilizing an adaptive multi-resolution lattice structure. It is specifically designed to address diffusion problems with arbitrary spatial and temporal scales and is adaptable to various diffusion types. Additionally, it is able to provide analytically exact solutions for a variety of diffusion methods, and we demonstrate a typical application using the heat equation.

In our study, we explored the application of inductive learning on in-the-wrist sensors to identify mathematical expressions written by hand. To achieve this, we collected sensor data from participants while they wrote mathematical expressions on paper and used it to train a neural network. The model was then tested by having other people wear similar sensors and having them write mathematical expressions, after which our inductive learning system analyzed the sensor data it received to determine the written expressions. To account for the influence of movement, we developed a method to reduce data related to unnecessary motion and increased accuracy by combining this technique with a neural network. By combining these techniques, we achieved a 70% error rate reduction in identifying mathematical expressions. To address challenges related to handwriting variation, we applied a technique that enabled the model to generalize from the initial training data and adapted to new, previously unseen writing styles.

One critical step in speech creation involves determining the length of speech segments. Currently, a traditional technique called Xaver's median cutting is used, but it relies heavily on statistical methods and can be resource-intensive. To address this limitation, we propose a median-based approach for automatically determining speech segment lengths in multilingual speech databases. This method utilizes basic text search techniques to create a reference speech library and automatically calculates the ideal speech length. The effectiveness of this non-statistical algorithm was extensively tested on the TOSS speech creation database with distinct results showing a significant improvement in speech length creation efficiency. Notably, the speech lengths generated by this method closely matched those obtained through manual trimming. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the method's versatility in rapidly calculating speech lengths for multilingual speech databases at a rate of 1 hour for every 10 hours of speech.

Conservation planning needs up-to-date, accurate data on where species are found.  
Correlative species distribution models have proven beneficial but can be misleading if species are analyzed in isolation.  
A modular conspecific model and integrated multispecies model address these issues by accounting for within and between species spatial patterns.  
To make these models more accessible, we developed the spHabitat package in R for user-friendly spatial presence analysis.  
This package includes tools for data preparation, model fitting, evaluation, and prediction, allowing integration into the broader R ecological modeling ecosystem.

This technical report outlines the Skincare initiative's development, which aims to create an automated, interactive AI-powered skin diagnosis system that helps healthcare professionals and patients detect skin cancers and other dermatological conditions early on. Researchers from the University of Oxford collaborated with dermatologists and the NHS to gather extensive image and clinical data, documenting over 100,000 diverse skin images and corresponding diagnoses. The data was used to create the largest publicly accessible dataset for dermatology education and research. The Skincare initiative's AI model achieved exceptional accuracy in classifying dermoscopic images, and was also combined with expert knowledge and user-interaction elements to create a functional clinical decision support system for healthcare professionals. The system has demonstrated significant benefits in helping general practitioners and dermatologists diagnose aggressive melanomas, while also maintaining a high level of accuracy in distinguishing benign from malignant cases. The research and development of Skincare have paved the way for creating an advanced, user-friendly skin diagnosis tool.

To enhance the accuracy of cosmological redshift estimates, we have integrated a fully probabilistic variational autoencoder into modern classification methods for Type Ia supernovae. Given a collection of snapshots from the evolution of an object, we model this data as a one-dimensional time series and utilize our encoder to convert each snapshot into a latent probability distribution, which our stochastic decoder then apply the diagonal Lambert-W function to convert the LTW diagonal matrix into a diagonal matrix with positive values and apply element-wise the Lambert-W function to the right side of the equation, which we then use to calculate the cosine similarity between two time series, which we use to estimate the redshift.

A massive galaxy cluster acting as a gravitational lens has amplified our view of a distant, star-forming galaxy at over seven billion light-years away. Observations using a powerful radio telescope have revealed detailed wind-like patterns within this galaxy, covering large areas of over 1 kiloparsec across. Although the wind-like patterns generate significant radio emissions, they likely interact with the dust present in this galaxy, producing strong signals at their current frequency. This galaxy contains much higher star formation activity compared to typical galaxies of its size and may be centered around an especially bright and massive star, as suggested by other observations. The properties of this wind-like pattern, including its speed and origin, are consistent with it being driven by a massive, star-producing region near the center of this galaxy, and its data provides valuable insight into how galaxies form and evolve at a crucial period in its development.

The growth dynamics of turbulent plumes are impacted by heavy particles in several ways. These effects include a reduction in the dynamic kinematic model's buoyancy inversion time and an additional addition to the heavy particle added mass. To account for these factors, we introduce a heavy particle addition mass term and revise the conventional incorporation rate that is typically used in turbulent plumes. In this revision, we use a heavy particle addition mass dependent incorporation rate that is calibrated through direct numerical simulations of turbulent plumes. This model takes into account differences in turbulent energy and particle length scales, as well as energy transfer to heavy particle kinetic energy. Additionally, we present a new model for turbulent plume velocity propagation that is also validated by direct numerical simulations. These model improvements enable accurate description of turbulent plume dynamics and heavy particle transfer in environments with particle lengths comparable to or greater than the turbulence energy length scale.

Over the last decade, understanding how epidemics spread within networked systems 
has become a major area of study, originating from research into susceptible systems 
that could only have connections between two individuals. This paper expands 
beyond traditional models by investigating hypergraphs, which allow for interactions 
between groups of three or more individuals, and examines the threshold at which 
an epidemic stops spreading. Through analyzing superspreaders--groups with high infection 
rates--on both randomly generated and real-world datasets, the paper proposes a 
theoretical extinction threshold that accounts for the effects of superspreaders.

Recent studies discovered that single-layer $\ferromagnetic\criv3$ exhibits a stable ferromagnetic spin-valley polarization, whereas multi-layer $\ferromagnetic\criv3$ shows spin-orbit interaction at room temperature. This paper theoretically analyzes the layer-coupled properties of multi-layer $\ferromagnetic\criv3$ through micromagnetic simulation, focusing on how inter-layer exchange stiffness, anisotropy, and reduced band gap influence its spin texture. Consequently, researchers found that in-layer and inter-layer coupling in multi-layer $\fermagentic\criv3$ follows easy-axis antiferromagnetism with a helical component, attributed to the spin-orbit interaction, which overrides the exchange coupling at high temperatures. This results in a skyrmion-like spin texture at high temperatures, whereas calculations and previous studies indicated that easy-axis ferromagnetism with a complex in-plane structure dominates at low temperatures. Moreover, the spin-orbit interaction influences the spin texture, particularly the in-plane structure, based on the specific orientation of layer stacking, as supported by high-energy transmission electron microscopy studies. This provides valuable insights for tuning spin textures in 2D van der Waals magnetic materials with strong spin-orbit interaction and for developing innovative spintronics applications based on these materials.

The rotation of younger stars than the Sun is believed to evolve differently, potentially influencing their magnetic cycle behaviors. By assuming a specific relationship between rotational velocity and latitude, we found that the time it takes for stars to change their rotation from faster at the center to slower at the surface directly correlates with the period of magnetic cycles in dynamic models. As this correlation suggests, we predict that the magnetic cycles in stars like the T Tauri type may behave differently than in the main-sequence stars, potentially affecting how we understand the magnetic cycles across different types of stars.

Deep multimodal learning through the integration of multiple data types is gaining momentum, 
with the primary objective of shared representation learning across different modalities.
Current deep framework approaches, however, are limited by their sensitivity to 
missing data and complex inter-modal relationships. This study proposes a novel 
deep framework that utilizes k-fan functions to model complex omni-modal 
relationships and a Shrinkage kernel Bayes method to manage various data missing 
scenarios in the training set. The proposed framework, a k-fan deep multimodal 
framework with shared representations, enables the efficient sharing of information 
across multiple modalities, while maintaining the capability to handle partial 
data. Experimental results on 3 distinct datasets validate the proposed method, 
demonstrating its superior performance over state-of-the-art multimodal deep 
learning methods.

The McMini model verifier employs Dynamic-Ordering-Prevention (DPOR) to analyze threads in multi-threaded programs based on a particular happening order. However, its reliance on such an order means it only works on a subset of all possible thread interactions, requiring various input modifications to produce complete results. In response to this limitation, we introduce a significant upgrade to the original model, allowing it to automatically generate the complete set of possible dynamic ordering sets for a program without manual intervention. Our enhanced model, still rooted in DPOR and similar to the original, works on different types of program dependencies, keeping it compatible with a wide range of program types. Our model's results were put to a comprehensive competitive test with other program analysis tools and performed exceptionally well on the tool category.

In an effort to stop the spread of false information, governments have proposed limiting users' abilities to share messages on WhatsApp. The plan is to require users to log in and identify themselves, allowing the government to monitor suspicious activity. However, this idea may backfire, as it could actually accelerate the dissemination of misinformation. Our goal is to investigate the feasibility of this idea, using both fieldwork and a simulation model to understand the dynamics of information propagation within our team.

We analyze a population model featuring large families, based on a branching process with a finite gene pool. This process generates individuals of varying types, each possessing one of several possible alleles. Our research focuses on the prevalence spectrum of alleles within a large population, specifically examining how the prevalence of rare alleles and their presence in a sample relate. As the population size approaches infinity, a non-trivial law of large numbers applies, leading to allele frequency convergence. However, the behavior of rare alleles differs, prompting additional theoretical requirements. These requirements include identifying and comparing the probability distributions of allele inheritance in the population and measuring allele prevalence. The prevalence spectrum's properties are then investigated under various assumptions regarding population and allele dynamics. These estimations hold significant biological implications, including the ability to determine a quantitative relationship between allele frequency and sample data. This relationship allows for evaluation of rarity indicators, such as allelic prevalence given presence in the sample. The concepts discussed here relate to earlier work on prevalence spectra in neutral branching processes and a related concept called "habitat prevalence" developed in mathematical population genetics.

This paper introduces an attentive activation mechanism (AAM) designed to boost the effectiveness of spoof detection algorithms. Comprising two modules - a spatial one that examines spatial patterns in feature maps and a temporal module that analyzes temporal dynamics of activations, the AAM aims to enhance the discriminative power of underlying neural networks. We integrate the AAM into a state-of-the-art spoof detection system, the local-enhanced cosine-melted ensemble (LIME), and conduct comprehensive experiments using the ASVTS datasets. The results show the Local-AAM module yields consistent improvements, averaging a 4.19% boost in EER compared to Local, with the Top-K-AAM module delivering even greater improvements, with an average 6.21% increase in EER compared to Local.

We've developed a new class of supersymmetric inflation models with superior
properties. In standard Local Supersymmetry models, the gravitational sector
consists of three complex fields - heavy for two and one field suitable for
driving inflation. To simplify, we proposed earlier a method involving the
separation of the two heavy fields using a locally supersymmetric version of
the Goldstone equivalence theorem. This effectively reduces the gravitational
sector's complexity without adding extra assumptions. Furthermore, we now
apply the same logic to isolate the scalar component within the remaining
gravitational field, leaving us with a locally supersymmetric model consisting
of a specific 'light' field within the gravitational sector, along with a
predictably monomial form for the inflaton's potential. These new models are
not only mathematically elegant but also make precise predictions for
cosmological parameters with enhancements to reheating and decay rates.

When associated with a non-parity symmetric pump pulse, the spatiotemporal mode of signal (or idler) photons influences the spectral mode of the opposing photons in a spontaneous spectral correlation process. This phenomenon is studied in experiments using spectral correlations of signal and idler photons and is observed to occur due to the interaction with the complex amplitude structure of the pump pulse. Moreover, the symmetry of the pump pulse determines the symmetry of the correlation. A nonlinear phase matching and the conservation of longitudinal momentum also play a crucial longitudinal momentum.

Our experiment employs terahertz spectroscopy and near-field microscopy to analyze the electromagnetic field distributions within superconducting microwave resonators and their coupling with optical photons. By mapping the field patterns of two types of resonators, we confirm calculated models and measure optical coupling coefficients, achieving a calculated value of approximately 99.9999994 percent for a high-performance resonator. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of utilizing superconducting circuits at optical frequencies and paves the way for exploring terahertz physics through superconducting quantum engineering.

We investigate how to partition the set of all real numbers into a collection of sets, with each set containing elements assigned the same value, based on a given property of interest. The first part of our research focuses on properties belonging to a specific hierarchy level within the set of all sets with measurable cardinality, demonstrating that such a partition yields a high category set of interest. This result extends an earlier finding by Bartoszewski regarding Lebesgue measure and builds upon work by Brendle, Kanamori, and Sliwowski regarding Borel sets. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between this partition and sets with particular membership in that hierarchy. A similar analysis is conducted for measures defined by assigning a particular probability to sets containing only countable or maximal cardinality sets, showing the partition yields a high category set of interest while the complement yields a low category set, all while remaining measurable with respect to the associated measure.

In recent years, there has been significant growth in the use of agent-based models in finance. These models replicate the actions of multiple agents to provide insights into the dynamics of the financial markets. Despite their utility, the unique contributions of agent-based models to the broader modeling approach remain unclear. This research aims to clarify this contribution. It analyzes the returns generated by different strategies when used in conjunction with agent-based models.

This study examines the effectiveness of two publicly available software tools, suricata and signature-based intrusion detection systems, in identifying and recognizing network protocols. These tools rely on signatures to detect anomalies, similar to how medical diagnostic systems rely on symptoms to identify diseases. Our research reveals that these tools are susceptible to being deceived into misidentifying network protocols when presented with malicious traffic patterns. Specifically, we found that these tools can incorrectly classify network protocols and, in some cases, fail to detect intrusions altogether.

We investigate how superconducting islands impact the flow of low-energy magnons in a thin film with exchange bias. Our key finding is that superconducting regions hinder the movement of magnons, similar to how barriers obstruct particles in the quantum world. This occurrence stems from the intense reflection of magnons at the interface with superconducting areas. It can be quantified by a distinct length scale related to magnon-phton interactions with superconductors. We further demonstrate that this phenomenon is most significant at lower temperatures, where the interface reflection dominates over the increasing superconducting gap. Moreover, engineering a periodic arrangement of ferromagnetic and superconducting layers could lead to the creation of a Bloch spectral function for magnons, analogous to electrons in quantum wells.

Audio event detection has made significant strides in recent years, particularly in frameworks like ADOS that have set new standards for performance. This progress has been largely driven by large, well-annotated datasets, such as ESC50 and ES21K, which have provided benchmarks for development. However, creating such datasets is both labor-intensive and expensive, and they are unlikely to be exhaustive due to the constant emergence of new categories. Consequently, developing methods to tackle this issue has become crucial for the field.

One challenge in addressing this problem lies in the difficulty of learning audio representations from scratch. While image recognition benefits from robust visual features, audio classifications often lack this advantage. Furthermore, the availability of computing power required to train these models individually would be inaccessible to most users.

Our research addresses this challenge by proposing ZFED, a novel method for zero-shot learning that utilizes federated averaging to combine local datasets without centralization. This is achieved by using ZFED to create acoustic representations and train classifiers simultaneously.

In our experiments, we evaluated the effectiveness of ZFED using ESC-50 and ES21K as training sources, while using DEC21 as the testing dataset. Additionally, we conducted further testing with DEC-10, a subset of DEC21 not included in ES21K.

Our results indicate that both ZFED and ZFEDStar significantly outperformed other methods in various settings, demonstrating an average improvement of 6.6

There is a need for effective verification methods for multi-particle entangled states across various fields of quantum research. A random sampling method is used to estimate the fidelity of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states in multiple dimensions, addressing both the rapid growth of experimental dimensions and the associated burden of measurement data. The approach randomizes the computation by selecting and evaluating specific computational bases based on available measurement data, significantly reducing the required number of samples for accurate fidelity estimation. The efficiency of this random sampling is enhanced by incorporating an optimization process that targets the most informative samples, further reducing the required sample size by accounting for the inherent variability in fidelity estimates. A complementary optimization and data analysis method is used to assess the reliability of the fidelity estimation within a desired confidence level. The proposed approach has been successfully applied to simulated data from quantum network experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in efficiently verifying complex, high-dimensional entangled states.

A cost-effective and low-complexity approach is proposed for estimating the wireless communication link in an outdoor environment featuring a reflective surface. Initially, the direct line-of-sight and reflective paths are assessed using a limited number of antennas, followed by the exploitation of a sparse reflective channel model to minimize the pilot signal requirement. Subsequently, the complete reflective channel is inferred through interpolation, followed by the verification of the estimation's accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's ability to provide accurate estimations with significantly reduced complexity compared to traditional approaches.

This research examines the correlation between media reporting on the COVID-19 pandemic and public and political responses across eight U.S. regions. Utilizing a dataset of over 1.3 million news articles from local publications, we analyzed media coverage, audience size, case numbers, and mortality rates, finding that media reporting on the pandemic, particularly in terms of case counts and fatalities, is correlated with both public and political outcomes such as mortality rates, case growth, mayoral re-elections, and mayoral re-endorsements. Interestingly, media behavior appears to be influenced by pandemic statistics, which in turn, is potentially affecting public and political decisions. To better understand this relationship and its potential implications, we used control variables such as control deaths, media exposure, control news volume, and demographic factors.

The fundamental skill of counting is a crucial aspect of cognitive development that supports a child's cognitive growth. Recent research has led to children's exposure to counting through the use of digital tools. However, the underlying processes of learning to count remain unclear. The present study focuses on counting progression from age three to four, given that these children experience a significant breakthrough in understanding the relationship between number words and meaning. The study's primary objective is to identify key factors that influence the acquisition of counting skills in typical children. To achieve this, the researchers constructed a neural network model to simulate the observed patterns of skill acquisition. The model's parameters were then adjusted to reflect variations in underlying cognitive abilities. The results indicated that these differences arise due to the varying rates at which children learn to integrate new information.

Bloom filters provide an approximate method for identifying set membership, with Bloom filter variation xBloom filters offering an improved, albeit still inexact, approach using bit-vector storage. Notably, xor filters represent an even faster and more efficient xBloom filter variant. Our test results reveal an exact Bloom filter capacity of over 90 percent of a xor filter's size, and a xBloom filter of the same capacity as a hash table of a comparable capacity. Our analysis further shows a similar experience with query times for both structures. Our experiments in fact show a Bloom filter capacity of 95 percent of a hash table, and a xor filter capacity 105 percent higher. We developed an improved algorithm for a single probe insertion into xor filters and found significant reductions in their size. Our results demonstrate reduced requirements by over ten percent for both 64-bit and 128-bit query times.

This article explores connections between two areas of study: 
(i) coefficients of convex functions in power series expansions and 
(ia) volumes of specific sections of n-dimensional unit balls. 
Specific inequalities are proposed for the absolute values of these function coefficients. 
Moreover, mean values of the modulus of analytic functions defined on the n-dimensional complex unit ball are evaluated at power series points. 
Research references are linked within the article's conclusions.

To predict market trends, we have created an model that analyzes market transactions over time, taking into account the time sequence, execution cost, and number of shares per transaction. It's important to consider how these events unfold over time, as well as their spatial distribution, to gain valuable insights. The future has a significant impact on present decision-making processes.

To achieve this, we have developed a neural network based on conformal prediction that can ConOuplet the temporal and spatial dependencies of a dataset. It does so by creating an unbiased cost function that respects time, execution cost, and number of shares as well as spatial distribution. The proposed method enables us to identify market trends based on past events, which can then be used to inform trading strategies.

We have tested our model on three datasets representing different market trends and found that it outperforms existing models in terms of accuracy and accuracy efficiency. The results show that our model can accurately predict market trends based on past events, which can then be used to inform trading strategies.

Federated Learning (FL) has become an increasingly significant approach for preserving privacy in distributed machine learning and has garnered substantial research attention recently. To further ensure a trustworthy and robust FL system, we aim to protect participants from malicious server operations, data manipulation, and theft. In response to these concerns, we introduce FLVoogd, an enhanced FL framework, by integrating real-world innovations such as homomorphic encryption, secret sharing, and differential privacy. Furthermore, FLVoogd successfully reduces the computational overhead associated with existing methods, making them more practical for real-world applications.

Achieving robust autonomous navigation in real-world scenarios is a challenging task. To overcome this, Sim2Real techniques are employed to bridge the gap between simulated and actual environments. By using deep reinforcement learning, policies developed in a simulated environment can be effectively transferred to the real world. However, the process of transferring these policies often requires access to real-world ground truth data, which can be difficult to obtain for complex tasks like navigation. In this research, we present an innovative approach that utilizes image gradients extracted from simulations to generate synthetic ground truth data. This generated data is then used to fine-tune policies in the real world, eliminating the need to collect expensive ground truth information. Through rigorous evaluation on the Klanker benchmark, we demonstrate that our method significantly enhances policy transferability when moving from simulation to real-world applications.

The emergence of deepfake creates challenges both technically and socially, 
resulting in a pressing need for advanced strong deepfake identification. 
However, traditional deepfake identification is limited to content-specific 
scenarios. To address this, a novel weak-to-strong deepfake creation and 
identification framework, named WSDF, is proposed, allowing for a seamless 
transition from specific content to unrestricted deepfake creation and 
identification.

Weak-to-strong deepfake creation commences with the extraction of feature 
embeddings from source video and target domain images, followed by the 
construction of strong deepfake using a novel deepfake creation network 
AWDfF. A double fusion mechanism, incorporating structural and edge details, 
enables the generation of high-quality strong deepfakes. A key point encoder is 
introduced to facilitate cross-modal knowledge transfer, while adversarial 
training with discriminator D further enhances the overall deepfake quality.

To tackle the issue of specific source content limitation, feature mask 
projection FMP is utilized in weak-to-strong deepfake creation. This enables 
the direct projection of deepfake features onto m frames, which are then used 
as anchor frames for the strong deepfake feature SFF. Subsequently, the rest 
of the frames are regenerated using recurrent video deepfake creation RVDfF. 
Adversarial training with D and G ensures that the deepfake quality is

The existence of supercritical fluids like dissolved gases, which may be present in the deep atmospheres of sub-Neptune exoplanets, can also affect their transit signatures beyond what is currently predicted by main-sequence models. These dissolved gases likely reached their current states due to migrations from their initial locations to closer orbits around their host stars, which subsequently led to the accumulation of mass and the onset of atmospheric collapse. Planets with sufficient internal heat can maintain saturated gas in their atmospheres, which may be present in the STIS/Kepler-187c and GJ-347c transit signatures. However, the simulations of these transient signals, which are influenced by the absorption of light by dissolved gases, are also dependent on the equation of state of these dissolved gases. Researchers have proposed two possible equations of state for these dissolved gases, which are based on different models of fluid behavior. These simulations also suggest that the study of sub-Neptune transit signatures can also provide valuable insights into the unknown properties of these exotic environments, which are not yet fully explored.

We present pattern classification and feature extraction algorithms implemented using only local and temporal constraints. Our approach yields supervised learning capabilities for both fully connected and convolutional spiking neural networks, with the latter retaining its sparsity. Unlike previous methods, we eliminate the need for non-biological operations during training. Furthermore, we formulate our algorithms within a constrained optimization framework. Our results demonstrate effective performance on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets.

This report presents the submission details of a specific team, known as
Out of the Lexicon Challenge, for the open challenge held in NLPCopen 2021. The
team's submission revolves around the Multilingual Cross-domain Semantic Textual
Similarity task. With no prior language modeling experience within our group, the
submission showcases a straightforward, yet effective strategy adapted from prior
successful submissions in related English-based challenges. Our approach involved
utilizing fine-tuned sentence-transformer models. Specifically, we employed the multi
language version of the cross-encoder model sentience as our primary method, also
complementing it with parallel sentence-transformers to account for potential ranking
issues.

This study introduces a novel verification technique for Generalized Polynomial Chaos expansions based on the residual of a generalized defect. A generalized residual expansion is proposed to identify and quantify the dominant sources contributing to the residual, enabling the assessment of the suitability of a PC approximation by measuring its mean square error. This concept is demonstrated through the simulation of two dynamical systems influenced by random factors: the former involves the random propagation of a wave in a bounded area, while the latter examines the propagation of waves in the same space under the influence of random media conditions.

This paper introduces an innovative adaptive control method specifically designed for systems with hidden state changes and one that can handle uncertainty. The approach utilizes a combination of a bank of adaptive dynamic regulators (BADRs) integrated with a residual evaluator (RE) to identify and adapt to state changes occurring within the system. The BADR bank generates a remaining signal which is then processed by the RE to detect state changes. The method effectively handles partial observability by using the maximum a posteriori probability and by limiting the impact of noise and uncertainty on its decision-making process through the application of a probabilistic constraint. In particular, noise and uncertainty are confined to a defined probabilistic boundary. The theoretical analysis proves that the proposed algorithm is capable of guaranteeing the perfect identification and adaptation of state changes occurring within the system while adhering to the imposed probabilistic constraint. The proposed control method has been successfully tested on a partial observation model representing a heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system.

The analysis of light from distant galaxies enables astronomers to trace the pace of star formation over vast periods, revealing valuable information about the universe's evolution over time. To achieve this, spectroscopy is employed to break down light into its component colors, allowing for precise measurements of stellar velocities, temperatures, and chemical makeups. The following discussion explores the significance of these measurements, the advancement of techniques in spectroscopy, and the insights they provide into the evolution of galaxies, particularly those of smaller size. The focus then shifts to specific examples, including the characteristics of these small galaxies and their star populations, before exploring the evolution of a particular type of small galaxy and their potential connection to larger galaxies. The analysis ultimately reveals the importance of studying these smaller galaxies in understanding the broader patterns of galaxy evolution over vast periods of time.

Given a continuous action of a profinite group $G$ on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, we can define a action spectrum, which is a function from the dual space of irreducible complex characters of $G$ to the integers. This action spectrum satisfies key properties: it is $G$-invariant under conjugation, stable under equivariant compactifications, and respects disjoint unions of spaces under G-actions. Additionally, it satisfies an additive property when spaces are combined in a disjoint manner.

Organizations depend on advanced document analysis tools, such as Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision technologies, to automate the processing of complex, visually appealing documents like invoices and receipts. However, developing these solutions requires access to large volumes of labeled training data, which is a significant financial and time investment due to the need for human annotation. In this study, we investigate methods to minimize the annotation costs while maintaining high performance on difficult tasks. To this end, we develop a hybrid approach combining human and machine annotation, which involves dividing the annotation process into two phases. In the first phase, machine-generated labels are refined by human experts and utilized to enhance the performance of pre-trained models. In the second phase, these optimized models are applied to a larger dataset, substituting the need for extensive human annotation. To validate our hypothesis, we evaluate the proposed approach on visual invoice parsing with limited training data and discover that just 10% of the data yields results nearly as accurate as the full dataset, surpassing existing data-saving annotations strategies.

Our study on the interface between EuS and InAs is conducted with a EuS monolayer in a (001) configuration on both the top and bottom InAs surfaces. Utilizing slab simulations with an increased number of layers and calculations of the work function, we examine the electronic properties of the EuS/InAs system with varying EuS thickness. The results indicate that within a few EuS layers, the InAs band is isolated from the EuS band, and the work function converges. The work function, work function difference, and charge transfer are determined and found to depend on the EuS/InAs binding orientation. The work function of the EuS/InAs system is found to be lower than that of the individual materials, and the origin of this reduction is attributed to the presence of In states with s character, which are located above the Fermi level at the interface.

A significant result by Wadge demonstrates the relationship between Wadge classes, a concept that categorizes polynomial time boolean functions with equivalent acceptance properties. Specifically, for any two such classes, either one is a subset of the other, or one is a subset of the other when considering their counterparts with optimal strategies for counter changes. Although this theorem has been known for some time, the existing proof is complex and relies on an intermediate, simpler version of the theorem. This simpler version states that either a subset relationship exists, a subset relationship exists with the described transformations, or a subset relationship exists also with the described transformations. An efficient proof for this simplified theorem is provided, which uses priority queue based structures to construct a deterministic machine that decides the corresponding language, thereby showing the desired reduction.

Deep neural networks (DNNs), predominantly employed to address a range of real-world issues due to their strong representation capabilities, have had their computation complexity significantly constrained by hardware limitations. The resulting constraint has hindered the application of DNNs in many critical scenarios. Pruning, a technique aimed at simplifying DNNs, has the potential to alleviate this issue, yet existing pruning techniques have inherent shortcomings. Some prune untargeted weights while others have low update efficiency. To address these limitations, ClickTrain is introduced - a fine-detail, end-to-end pruning algorithm that surpasses the advantages of training-parallelism, supports the pruning of any weight without restriction, and has a lower update cost. The results indicate ClickTrain exceeds the state-of-the-art pruning methods on benchmark tasks, including image classification and neural machine translation.

This study integrates modal operators into the Ld calculus, a nonassociative logic system. The Ld calculus models aspectual behavior but lacks mechanisms to capture generative or change-of-state behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce new rules utilizing modal operators to establish $\Box$-rule and introduce the Ld(\b) calculus. The Ld(\b) calculus is shown to be complete with respect to its semantic meaning, a result derived from a process of proving the completeness of the \Box rule. The proof involves an adaptation of the potential tree technique, specifically a modal version, to an extended framework of lambda terms.

The observation of neutron star-black hole collisions via gravitational waves offers a singular opportunity to study physical phenomena, but the associated signals are complicated by the presence of neutron star matter, which can't be fully captured by standard approaches. These features, while subtle, are expected to be detectable in the chirp parameters of the gravitational wave signals, particularly if the black hole is not overly massive. To investigate this uncertainty, researchers have used simulated data to analyze the detectability of these characteristics through standard and machine learning methods. The analysis revealed that, for optimal detection, the neutron star should remain intact and evaporate into radiation before the merger occurs, which can happen if the neutron star is close to the black hole's horizon and certain conditions are met. The study also found that, even if the merger happens earlier, the associated features can still be detected by advanced detectors. To aid in the categorization of the signals, researchers have employed a machine learning approach, which has shown success in identifying the parameters and masses of the black hole and neutron star.

Our analysis of the Kepler observations reveals a transiting exoplanet, designating it as TOI-5542b. Through our modeling of the planet's passage across its host star, we calculate a planet radius of approximately $1.147 \pm 0.009$ Jupiter radii and a mass estimate of $2.73_{-1.99}^{+5.57}$ Mj. The resulting estimate for the planet's density is $0.74 \pm 0.13$ g/cm$^3$. Based on the planet's passage across its host star, we calculate an orbital period of $471.94 \pm 0.47$ days and a semi-major axis of $2.99 \pm 0.12$ AU. The planet is modeled as a hot Jupiter with hot Neptune characteristics due to the lack of detected tidal effects. By examining the patterns in the planet's position, we determine a parallax of $0.54 \pm 0.19$ mas and an extinction of $0.31 \pm 0.04$ AU due to the planet's movement. This research explores a restricted version of Markov decision processes, 
where state transitions in the underlying stochastic process, 
after a certain time period, are based on a known probability distribution 
independent of past actions and states. Beginning with key applications in 
privacy-preserving environments, we introduce an optimization framework for 
primary dual variables, leading to significant computational efficiency. 
By breaking down this constrained problem into simpler issues involving 
correlation matrices, we can apply well-established methods from linear programming. 
Our approach requires solving standard linear programs, for which there are 
many efficient solution methods, thus addressing the scalability issues. 
We demonstrate the practical applicability of this framework through testing 
on privacypreserving healthcare and transportation use cases, showing that 
it scales to large problems commonly encountered.

This research introduces an advanced optical character recognition system for accurately identifying handwritten mathematical symbols and equations, excluding text characters. The method leverages a neural network to extract handwritten symbols, which are then combined with pre-existing data and used to create a classification model. The model is optimized to optimize its performance and tested on an advanced file, creating a equation parsing algorithm. The proposed system shows outstanding results and a file availability of 97%. The innovative handwritten symbol extraction technique and a vast, meticulously organized dataset of 12k mathematical notation are provided and available for character recognition tasks. The training data and code can be accessed at https://github.com/eqrecognition/equrecognition.
